rows.name: fifo-why
rows.question: Why does index equality alone not distinguish full from empty? Give the two concrete capacity-17 states and show how your actual implementation distinguishes them.
rows.recognizedQuestion: Why does index equality alone not distinguish full from empty? Give the two concrete capacity-17 states and show how your actual implementation distinguishes them.
rows.answer:
Equal read and write indices can mean either empty or full because advancing 17 positions wraps back to the same index. In this implementation, the write index is computed as `(head_ + size_) % capacity`; it is not stored separately.

Initially, `head_ = 0` and `size_ = 0`, so the write index is `(0 + 0) % 17 = 0`: both indices are 0, but the queue is empty and `pop` returns false.

After pushing values 0 through 16, `head_ = 0` and `size_ = 17`, so the write index is `(0 + 17) % 17 = 0`: both indices are again 0, but all 17 slots are occupied and the next `push` returns false without changing anything.

The invariant is `0 <= size_ <= 17`, with queued items at `(head_ + k) % 17` for `0 <= k < size_`. Thus `size_ == 0` distinguishes empty from `size_ == 17`, which means full.

review.note: Actual implementation computes write index from head+size: empty(0,0) and full(0,17) both imply same index; count distinguishes. Does not invent a separately stored tail.
review.usefulPrefix: Equal read and write indices can mean either empty or full because advancing 17 positions wraps back to the same index.

rows.name: floating-counterexample
rows.question: Under IEEE binary32, round after each addition and forbid reassociation. Evaluate (16777216 + -16777216) + 1 and 16777216 + (-16777216 + 1). Then change the leftmost operand to positive 16777216, the middle operand to 1, and the last operand to -16777216. Compare both parenthesizations of that changed triple. Explain representability at each intermediate step; do not simply cite nonassociativity.
rows.recognizedQuestion: Under IEEE binary32, round after each addition and forbid reassociation. Evaluate (16777216 + -16777216) + 1 and 16777216 + (-16777216 + 1). Then change the leftmost operand to positive 16777216, the middle operand to 1, and the last operand to -16777216. Compare both parenthesizations of that changed triple. Explain representability at each intermediate step; do not simply cite nonassociativity.
rows.answer:
Using IEEE binary32’s default rounding mode, round-to-nearest, ties-to-even, the original triple gives 1 with both parenthesizations; the changed triple gives 0 on the left and 1 on the right.

Original triple:
• (16777216 + -16777216) + 1: the first addition gives exactly 0, then exactly 1. Both intermediate results are representable.
• 16777216 + (-16777216 + 1): the inner result is exactly -16777215, which is representable; adding 16777216 then gives exactly 1.

Changed triple:
• (16777216 + 1) + -16777216: the exact inner sum, 16777217, is not representable. At and above 16777216, adjacent binary32 values are spaced 2 apart, so it lies halfway between 16777216 and 16777218. Ties-to-even rounds it to 16777216; the final addition gives exactly 0.
• 16777216 + (1 + -16777216): the inner result is exactly -16777215 and is representable, because integers with magnitude below 16777216 have sufficient precision. The final addition therefore gives exactly 1.

The key is that 16777217 is not representable, whereas -16777215 is. Rounding each addition in the specified order—not reassociating—produces the difference.

review.note: States ties-even assumption; original pair both1 because-16777215 exactly representable; changed triple left0/right1 because16777217 ties rounds2^24. Reasoning traces each intermediate.
review.usefulPrefix: Using IEEE binary32’s default rounding mode, round-to-nearest, ties-to-even, the original triple gives 1 with both parenthesizations; the changed triple gives 0 on the left and 1 on the right.

rows.name: quorum-counterexample
rows.question: Five replicas A,B,C,D,E retain the highest version. A writer finishes after three acknowledgements. A reader queries any three and returns the highest version, without write-back. Prove or disprove linearizability including reads overlapping an incomplete write: give a fully ordered execution with two nonoverlapping reads and show the attempted linearization contradiction. Then change only the reader to write the selected version to three replicas before returning and explain whether this fixes the counterexample.
rows.recognizedQuestion: Five replicas A,B,C,D,E retain the highest version. A writer finishes after three acknowledgements. A reader queries any three and returns the highest version, without write-back. Prove or disprove linearizability including reads overlapping an incomplete write: give a fully ordered execution with two nonoverlapping reads and show the attempted linearization contradiction. Then change only the reader to write the selected version to three replicas before returning and explain whether this fixes the counterexample.
rows.answer:
Without read write-back, this is not linearizable: two nonoverlapping reads can return a new version and then an old one.

Initially, A,B,C,D,E all store version 0. Consider this fully ordered execution:
1. Writer W invokes a write of version 1.
2. A stores version 1 and acknowledges. All other write messages remain delayed, so W has only one acknowledgement and is incomplete.
3. R1 is invoked, queries A,B,C, and receives versions 1,0,0. R1 returns 1.
4. After R1 returns, R2 is invoked, queries B,C,D, and receives versions 0,0,0. R2 returns 0.
5. Only afterward, deliver W’s messages to B and C; both store 1 and acknowledge, allowing W to finish.

To explain R1’s result in a sequential register history, W must be linearized before R1. Real-time order requires R1 before R2. Thus W must precede R2, which must return 1, not 0: a contradiction. Even if W remains pending forever, omitting it cannot explain R1’s return of 1, and including it creates the same contradiction.

Requiring the reader to write back its selected version and receive acknowledgements from three replicas before returning fixes this counterexample. If R1 selects 1, its completed write-back leaves at least three replicas holding version 1 or higher. Every subsequent three-replica read intersects that set because 3 + 3 > 5; replicas never decrease their versions, so R2 cannot return 0.

With a single writer issuing increasing versions, this is the standard read-repair quorum construction for a linearizable register: completed writes and completed reads both establish a quorum that prevents later reads from going backward. For multiple writers, that broader guarantee additionally requires a correct globally ordered, unique version-tag generation protocol; read write-back alone does not supply it.

review.note: Concrete A-only incomplete write; R1ABC1 then R2BCD0 nonoverlap; later Wcompletion optional. Read write-back fixes quorum inversion, broad single/multiple-writer qualification explicit.
review.usefulPrefix: Without read write-back, this is not linearizable: two nonoverlapping reads can return a new version and then an old one.

rows.name: quorum-why
rows.question: Why does the second read have to respect a value returned by the first read even if the writer never completed? State the relevant real-time order and distinguish it from requiring every unfinished operation to complete.
rows.recognizedQuestion: Why does the second read have to respect a value returned by the first read even if the writer never completed? State the relevant real-time order and distinguish it from requiring every unfinished operation to complete.
rows.answer:
Because the first read completed before the second read began, linearizability requires R1 before R2 in the sequential history. If R1 returns the new value, the pending write must be included and placed before R1 to explain that result; with no intervening write, R2 cannot then return the old value.

This does not require every unfinished operation to complete. Pending operations may be omitted or supplied with responses when constructing a linearization, but omitting this particular write would leave R1’s new value unexplained. Thus the required order is write < R1 < R2, even though the writer never actually returned.

review.note: Pending operation can be omitted or completed only in construction of linearization; R1newvalue forces inclusion and order W<R1<R2; no obligation to make actual writer finish.
review.usefulPrefix: Because the first read completed before the second read began, linearizability requires R1 before R2 in the sequential history.
